claim: PCGF1-PRC1 is a highly abundant complex in embryonic cells and tissues where the PcG system plays a pivotal role in developmental gene regulation.
source: In embryonic cells and tissues where the PcG system is thought to play a pivotal role in developmental gene regulation, the PCGF1-PRC1 complex is highly abundant (Kloet et al., 2016), and is required for H2AK119ub1 and normal development (Farcas et al., 2012; Blackledge et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013; Gearhart et al., 2006; Boulard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: PCGF1-PRC1 is required for H2AK119ub1 and normal development.
source: In embryonic cells and tissues where the PcG system is thought to play a pivotal role in developmental gene regulation, the PCGF1-PRC1 complex is highly abundant (Kloet et al., 2016), and is required for H2AK119ub1 and normal development (Farcas et al., 2012; Blackledge et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013; Gearhart et al., 2006; Boulard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex contains five components: RING1B, PCGF1, RYBP, KDM2B and BCOR.
source: To achieve this, we used a baculovirus co-expression system (Bieniossek et al., 2012) to assemble and affinity-purify the five component PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex containing RING1B, PCGF1, RYBP, KDM2B and BCOR (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated through protein purification and visualization in Figure 1A and B

claim: RING1B is in close proximity to PCGF1 and RYBP within the PCGF1-PRC1 complex.
source: For example, RING1B was in close proximity to PCGF1 and RYBP.
evidence: Determined by crosslinking mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: RING1B and RYBP crosslinks are consistent with atomic resolution information detailing their physical interaction.
source: Importantly RING1B and RYBP crosslinks were consistent with atomic resolution information detailing their physical interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Crosslinking data validated against known crystal structure and published literature

claim: BCOR and KDM2B crosslink extensively with each other, suggesting they are in close proximity within the PCGF1-PRC1 complex.
source: BCOR and KDM2B crosslinked extensively with each other suggesting they are in close proximity and also displayed additional crosslinks with PCGF1 and RYBP.
evidence: Determined by crosslinking mass spectrometry analysis

claim: There is no evidence for significant crosslinks between either BCOR or KDM2B and RING1B, suggesting they are not in close proximity within the complex.
source: However, there was no evidence for significant crosslinks between either BCOR or KDM2B and RING1B, suggesting they are not in close proximity within the complex.
evidence: Based on absence of crosslinks in mass spectrometry data

claim: The PCGF1-PRC1 complex exhibits a high degree of modularity where individual combinations of proteins engage extensively with each other, while others exhibit little or no clear proximity.
source: This suggests a high degree of modularity within the PCGF1-PRC1 complex, where individual combinations of proteins engage extensively with each other, while others exhibit little or no clear proximity.
evidence: Inferred from crosslinking mass spectrometry data showing differential protein proximities

claim: KDM2B and BCOR can be completely removed from the PCGF1-PRC1 complex, either individually or in combination, to leave an intact PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP sub-complex.
source: This revealed that KDM2B and BCOR, which appear to interact with the complex through PCGF1 (Figure 1C), can be completely removed, either individually or in combination, to leave an intact PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP sub-complex (Figure 1D(i–iii)).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression experiments shown in Figure 1D

claim: When RYBP is removed from the PCGF1-PRC1 complex, BCOR and KDM2B are still able to independently interact with the PCGF1-RING1B dimer.
source: Similarly, when RYBP was removed from the PCGF1-PRC1 complex, BCOR and KDM2B were still able to independently interact with the PCGF1-RING1B dimer (Figure 1D(iv–v)).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression experiments shown in Figure 1D

claim: The inclusion of BCOR and KDM2B in the PCGF1-PRC1 complex does not require RYBP or an interaction with each other.
source: This indicates that inclusion of BCOR and KDM2B in the PCGF1-PRC1 complex does not require RYBP, or an interaction with each other.
evidence: Inferred from co-expression experiments showing independent interactions

claim: PCGF1 and RING1B form dimers in the absence of other PCGF1-PRC1 components.
source: Finally, in agreement with analysis of other PCGF/RING1 interactions, PCGF1/RING1B formed dimers in the absence of other PCGF1-PRC1 components (Figure 1D(vi)).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression experiments and consistent with published literature on other PCGF/RING1 interactions

claim: The PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex assembles around a core PCGF1-RING1B dimer in a highly modular fashion.
source: Therefore, the PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex assembles around a core PCGF1-RING1B dimer, and does so in a highly modular fashion.
evidence: Concluded from the series of co-expression experiments showing independent assembly of subunits

claim: The Drosophila dRAF complex exhibits similar modularity to PCGF1-PRC1.
source: Interestingly, in Drosophila, the related dRAF complex exhibits similar modularity (Lagarou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The assembly of PCGF1-PRC1 contrasts with the assembly of the PRC2 holocomplex, which relies on extensive and highly integrated protein-protein interactions for its efficient formation.
source: This contrasts the assembly of the PRC2 holocomplex, which appears to rely on extensive and highly integrated protein-protein interactions for its efficient formation (Ciferri et al., 2012; Jiao and Liu, 2015).
evidence: Comparison based on published literature about PRC2 assembly

claim: Reconstituted PCGF1-PRC1 is active in converting H2A to mono-ubiquitylated H2A.
source: To address this important question, we first established a quantitative in vitro E3 ligase activity assay using nucleosome substrates and confirmed that reconstituted PCGF1-PRC1 was active by detecting the conversion of H2A to mono-ubiquitylated H2A (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro E3 ligase assay shown in Figure 2A

claim: The PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex is substantially more active than the PCGF1-RING1B core dimer.
source: Surprisingly, the PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex was substantially more active than the PCGF1-RING1B core (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative E3 ligase activity assay shown in Figure 2B

claim: Interaction of RYBP with the RING1B-PCGF1 core dimer is responsible for elevated enzymatic activity of the PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex.
source: This revealed that interaction of RYBP with the RING1B-PCGF1 core dimer was responsible for elevated enzymatic activity of the PCGF1-PRC1 holocomplex.
evidence: Determined by testing individual PCGF1-PRC1 sub-complexes in E3 ligase assays shown in Figure 2C

claim: KDM2B and BCOR contribute little or nothing to the E3 ligase activity of PCGF1-PRC1.
source: In contrast, KDM2B and BCOR appeared to contribute little or nothing to this activity, suggesting that they confer alternative, non-enzymatic functions to the PRC1 complex.
evidence: Determined by testing sub-complexes lacking these components in E3 ligase assays

claim: YAF2 stimulates PCGF1-RING1B activity.
source: Importantly, this revealed that YAF2 also stimulated PCFG1-RING1B activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by E3 ligase assay with recombinant YAF2 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: RYBP and YAF2 regulate PCGF1-PRC1 activity in vitro by stimulating the PCGF1-RING1B core dimer and enhancing H2AK119ub1 deposition.
source: Together these observations reveal that RYBP and YAF2 regulate PCGF1-PRC1 activity in vitro, where they act to stimulate the PCGF1-RING1B core dimer and enhance H2AK119ub1 deposition.
evidence: Concluded from E3 ligase assays with RYBP and YAF2

claim: PCGF1-RING1B is significantly more active than PCGF4-RING1B.
source: Interestingly, this revealed that PCGF1-RING1B was significantly more active than PCGF4-RING1B (Figure 3B), indicating that the enzymatic activity of a given PRC1 complex is inherently defined by the PCGF-RING dimer which forms its catalytic core.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative E3 ligase assay shown in Figure 3B

claim: The enzymatic activity of a given PRC1 complex is inherently defined by the PCGF-RING dimer which forms its catalytic core.
source: Interestingly, this revealed that PCGF1-RING1B was significantly more active than PCGF4-RING1B (Figure 3B), indicating that the enzymatic activity of a given PRC1 complex is inherently defined by the PCGF-RING dimer which forms its catalytic core.
evidence: Inferred from comparative activity data between PCGF1-RING1B and PCGF4-RING1B

claim: RYBP has a small stimulatory effect on PCGF4-RING1B activity.
source: In the context of our experiments, we observe a small stimulatory effect when RYBP was added to PCGF4-RING1B (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by E3 ligase assay shown in Figure 3B

claim: PCGF4-RING1B-RYBP is much less active than PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP.
source: Despite this low level of stimulation, PCGF4-RING1B-RYBP was still much less active than PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative E3 ligase assay data

claim: The PCGF component of PRC1 complexes defines the inherent H2AK119 E3 ligase activity of individual PRC1 dimers.
source: Together these observations indicate that the PCGF component of the PRC1 complexes defines the inherent H2AK119 E3 ligase activity of individual PRC1 dimers and that inclusion of RYBP/YAF2 further matures these assemblies into robust enzymes that can efficiently modify chromatin.
evidence: Concluded from comparative activity assays of different PCGF-containing complexes

claim: Inclusion of RYBP/YAF2 matures PRC1 assemblies into robust enzymes that can efficiently modify chromatin.
source: Together these observations indicate that the PCGF component of the PRC1 complexes defines the inherent H2AK119 E3 ligase activity of individual PRC1 dimers and that inclusion of RYBP/YAF2 further matures these assemblies into robust enzymes that can efficiently modify chromatin.
evidence: Concluded from E3 ligase assays showing RYBP/YAF2 stimulation

claim: Both wildtype RYBP and RYBP with mutations in the NZF domain that abrogate ubiquitin binding stimulate the activity of PCGF1-RING1B to a similar extent.
source: Importantly, both forms of RYBP stimulated the activity of PCGF1-RING1B to a similar extent (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by E3 ligase assay comparing wildtype and mutant RYBP shown in Figure 4B

claim: The ability of RYBP to recognise ubiquitin does not account for its stimulation of PRC1.
source: Given that the ability of RYBP to recognise ubiquitin did not account for its stimulation of PRC1, we wondered whether RYBP may instead affect how the core dimer assembles to function as an H2AK119 E3 ligase.
evidence: Inferred from data showing ubiquitin-binding mutant RYBP retains stimulatory activity

claim: Within the PCGF1-RING1B dimer, there are multiple high-confidence crosslinks between the RING domain of RING1B and its C-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain, suggesting significant intramolecular interactions between these regions.
source: Within the PCGF1-RING1B dimer, we observed multiple high-confidence crosslinks between the RING domain of RING1B and its C-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain, suggesting that there are likely significant intramolecular interactions occurring between these regions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Determined by crosslinking mass spectrometry shown in Figure 4C

claim: Most of the RING domain/RING-UBL domain crosslinks within RING1B are lost in the trimeric complex (PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP).
source: Intriguingly, most of the RING domain/RING-UBL domain crosslinks within RING1B were lost in the trimeric complex (PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP) (Figure 4D), suggesting that RYBP causes an alteration in PCGF1-RING1B which limits association between its N- and C-terminal domains, possibly to stabilize the formation of an optimally assembled and active E3 ligase.
evidence: Determined by crosslinking mass spectrometry comparing dimer and trimer shown in Figure 4D

claim: RYBP causes an alteration in PCGF1-RING1B which limits association between its N- and C-terminal domains, possibly to stabilize the formation of an optimally assembled and active E3 ligase.
source: Intriguingly, most of the RING domain/RING-UBL domain crosslinks within RING1B were lost in the trimeric complex (PCGF1-RING1B-RYBP) (Figure 4D), suggesting that RYBP causes an alteration in PCGF1-RING1B which limits association between its N- and C-terminal domains, possibly to stabilize the formation of an optimally assembled and active E3 ligase.
evidence: Inferred from crosslinking mass spectrometry data showing loss of intramolecular crosslinks upon RYBP binding

claim: RYBP helps to reconfigure and stabilize the PCGF1-RING1B dimer.
source: This is in agreement with our crosslinking mass spectrometry analysis, and suggests that RYBP helps to reconfigure and stabilize the PCGF1-RING1B dimer.
evidence: Inferred from crosslinking data and reduced PCGF1 levels in absence of RYBP

claim: Reduced PCGF1 inclusion does not explain the effect that RYBP has on the activity of PCGF1/PRC1 complexes.
source: Importantly however, reduced PCGF1 inclusion does not explain the effect that RYBP has on the activity of PCGF1/PRC1 complexes, as the presence of RYBP stimulated the relative activity of PRC1 to a much larger extent than can be simply explained by PCGF1 levels alone (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of activity data with PCGF1 levels

claim: RYBP and YAF2 can significantly stimulate the activity of pre-existing PCGF1-RING1B assemblies.
source: Furthermore, RYBP and YAF2 were able to significantly stimulate the activity of pre-existing PCGF1-RING1B assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by E3 ligase assay with recombinant RYBP/YAF2 added to purified PCGF1-RING1B

claim: Treatment of Rybpfl/fl;Yaf2−/− cells with tamoxifen for 96 hr results in a complete loss of RYBP protein.
source: Treatment of the Rybpfl/fl;Yaf2−/− cell line with tamoxifen resulted in a complete loss of RYBP by 96 hr as assessed by western blot (Figure 5B) and at PcG targets as assessed by ChIP-seq (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and ChIP-seq shown in Figures 5B and 5C

claim: Deletion of RYBP in Rybpfl/fl;Yaf2−/− cells does not lead to an appreciable reduction in total RING1B.
source: In the context or our new Rybpfl/fl;Yaf2−/−conditional system, deletion of RYBP did not lead to an appreciable reduction in total RING1B (Figure 5B), in agreement with our observation that PRC1 complex assembly in vitro is modular (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 5B

claim: Removal of RYBP in Rybpfl/fl;Yaf2−/− cells does not significantly affect total H2AK119ub1 as measured by western blot.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, despite the dramatic affects that RYBP has on H2AK119 E3 ligase activity in vitro, removal of RYBP did not significantly affect total H2AK119ub1 as measured by western blot (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot quantitation shown in Figures 5D and 5E

claim: H2AK119ub1 signal in wild-type cells is highly correlated with both RING1B and RYBP occupancy genome-wide.
source: Importantly, H2AK119ub1 signal in wild-type cells was highly correlated with both RING1B and RYBP occupancy genome-wide (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by genome-wide correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: Removal of RYBP results in clear reductions in H2AK119ub1 at individual Polycomb target sites.
source: When we compared the levels of H2AK119ub1 before and after RYBP removal at individual Polycomb target sites, we observed clear reductions in H2AK119ub1 (Figure 5G), suggesting that RYBP supports deposition of H2AK119ub1 at these genomic locations.
evidence: Demonstrated by calibrated ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5G

claim: Approximately 45% of H2AK119ub1-enriched regions show significant reductions in H2AK119ub1 following RYBP removal.
source: Quantitation of H2AK119ub1 after removal of RYBP revealed widespread effects on H2AK119ub1 (Figure 5H), with approximately 45% of regions showing significant reductions in the levels of H2AK119ub1 (1091/2407; p<0.05).
evidence: Quantified from calibrated ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5H

claim: Nearly all PRC1 targets display reductions in H2AK119ub1 following RYBP removal, albeit many below the significance threshold.
source: However, this appeared to be an underestimation of the effect, as nearly all PRC1 targets displayed reductions in H2AK119ub1, albeit below the significance threshold (Figure 5I).
evidence: Observed in scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 5I

claim: A proportion of total cellular H2AK119ub1 resides outside of classical polycomb target sites.
source: This is likely due to a proportion of total cellular H2AK119ub1 residing outside of classical polycomb target sites as has been proposed previously in other systems (Lee et al., 2015; Goldknopf et al., 1975).
evidence: Inferred from discrepancy between ChIP-seq and western blot results, supported by citations

claim: The majority of PRC1 target sites (78%; 1870/2407) fail to show a significant change in RING1B occupancy following RYBP deletion.
source: We extended this analysis genome-wide (Figure 6B), and found that the majority of PRC1 target sites (78%; 1870/2407) failed to show a significant change in RING1B occupancy (Figure 6B) and we validated these observations at a number of sites using ChIP quantitative PCR analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified from RING1B ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B and validated by ChIP-qPCR

claim: Following RYBP deletion, clear and widespread reductions in H2AK119ub1 occur at PRC1 target sites where RING1B occupancy remains unchanged.
source: Importantly, following RYBP deletion we observed clear and widespread reductions in H2AK119ub1 at PRC1 target sites where RING1B occupancy remained unchanged.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing H2AK119ub1 and RING1B ChIP-seq data

claim: RYBP stimulates the E3 ligase activity of PRC1 in vivo, and decreases in H2AK119ub1 at PRC1 target sites are not due to defects in targeting PRC1.
source: Together, these genome-wide observations strongly support our in vitro conclusions that RYBP stimulates the E3 ligase activity of PRC1, and reveal that decreases in H2AK119ub1 at PRC1 target sites are not due to defects in targeting PRC1.
evidence: Concluded from genome-wide ChIP-seq analysis showing H2AK119ub1 loss without RING1B loss

claim: Sites with limiting amounts of PRC1 have a more defined requirement for RYBP-dependent stimulation to achieve normal H2AK119ub1.
source: This suggests that sites with limiting amounts of PRC1 have a more defined requirement for RYBP-dependent stimulation to achieve normal H2AK119ub1.
evidence: Inferred from analysis showing sites with lowest RING1B have highest dependency on RYBP

claim: Sites where loss of RYBP most profoundly affects H2AK119ub1 exhibit the highest ratios of RYBP to RING1B.
source: This revealed that the sites where loss of RYBP most profoundly affected H2AK119ub1 exhibited the highest ratios of RYBP to RING1B (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of RYBP/RING1B ratios shown in Figures 7D and 7E

claim: Variant-enriched PRC1 targets tend to show the largest reductions in H2AK119ub1 following RYBP removal.
source: Indeed, PRC1 targets that were occupied by RYBP but displayed reduced levels of CBX7 (i.e. 'variant-enriched') tended to show the largest reductions in H2AK119ub1 following RYBP removal (Figure 7F and G), whereas variant and canonical PRC1 occupied sites (i.e. 'shared') appeared to rely on RYBP to a lesser extent.
evidence: Demonstrated by clustering analysis shown in Figures 7F and 7G

claim: Deletion of RYBP results in genome-wide reductions in H3K27me3 at Polycomb target sites.
source: Strikingly, deletion of RYBP resulted in genome-wide reductions in H3K27me3 at Polycomb target sites (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq shown in Figures 8A and 8B

claim: H3K27me3 reductions at Polycomb target sites following RYBP deletion occur without any apparent loss in the chromatin occupancy of the PRC2 component SUZ12.
source: Importantly, H3K27me3 reductions at Polycomb target sites occurred without any apparent loss in the chromatin occupancy of the PRC2 component SUZ12 (Figure 8A and C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the observed decreases in H3K27me3 likely arise as a result of reduced activity of the PRC2 complex.
evidence: Demonstrated by SUZ12 ChIP-seq shown in Figures 8A, 8C, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: The largest reductions in H3K27me3 following RYBP deletion are evident at variant-enriched PRC1 target sites.
source: Like the observed changes in H2AK119ub1 (Figure 7F and G), the largest reductions in H3K27me3 were evident at variant-enriched PRC1 target sites (Figure 8D), consistent with a more defined role for RYBP in maintaining PcG-associated histone marks at these regions.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 8D

claim: Reductions in H3K27me3 across all PRC1 target sites correlate closely with reductions in H2AK119ub1 following RYBP deletion.
source: Importantly, reductions in H3K27me3 across all PRC1 target sites correlated closely with reductions in H2AK119ub1 (Figure 8E), indicating that the effects on H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 are linked and directly related to the activity of RYBP.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8E

claim: RYBP-dependent H2AK119ub1 shapes the activity of PRC2 in depositing H3K27me3.
source: These important observations demonstrate that RYBP-dependent H2AK119ub1 shapes the activity of PRC2 in depositing H3K27me3, and suggests that the observed stimulation of PRC2 by nucleosomes containing H2A mono-ubiquitylation in vitro is also relevant in vivo (Kalb et al., 2014).
evidence: Concluded from correlation between H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 changes, supported by citation to in vitro work

claim: Sites with the most profound losses of H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 following RYBP deletion are the same sites that show reductions in PRC1 and PRC2 occupancy.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the sites with the most profound losses of H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 were the same sites that showed reductions in PRC1 and PRC2 (Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 8F

claim: There is an intimate relationship between the histone-modifying activities of PRC1 and PRC2 at target sites, which is regulated by auxiliary PcG complex subunits and not simply dictated by occupancy of PRC1/PRC2 core catalytic subunits.
source: Firstly, there is an intimate relationship between the histone-modifying activities of PRC1 and PRC2 at target sites, which is regulated by auxiliary PcG complex subunits and not simply dictated by occupancy of PRC1/PRC2 core catalytic subunits.
evidence: Concluded from observations that RYBP removal affects histone modifications without affecting core complex occupancy

claim: The occupancy of PcG complexes at target sites is not driven in a linear fashion by H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels.
source: Secondly, the occupancy of PcG complexes at target sites is not driven in a linear fashion by H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels.
evidence: Inferred from observation that most sites retain PcG occupancy despite reduced histone modifications

claim: If activity-based communication between PcG complexes is compromised, there appears to be a modification threshold below which complex occupancy can no longer be sustained.
source: However, if activity-based communication between the PcG complexes is compromised there appears to be a modification threshold below which complex occupancy can no longer be sustained.
evidence: Inferred from observation that sites with greatest histone modification loss also lose PcG occupancy

claim: Loss of RYBP results in a limited number of robust and statistically significant transcriptional changes.
source: This revealed that loss of RYBP resulted in a limited number of robust and statistically significant transcriptional changes (Figure 9A), in agreement with previous studies examining gene expression by microarray analysis in RYBP deleted cells (Hisada et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9A and consistent with published literature

claim: More genes are significantly upregulated (n = 230) than downregulated (n = 37) following RYBP deletion.
source: Consistent with a role for RYBP in shaping PRC1-dependent gene repression, more genes were significantly upregulated (n = 230) than downregulated (n = 37), and these tended to be lowly expressed genes (Figure 9A).
evidence: Quantified from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 9A

claim: Most RYBP-repressed genes fall within the set of genes that are also regulated by RING1A/B.
source: Furthermore, when we compared these gene expression changes to those observed in the complete absence of PRC1 activity (RING1A−/−;RING1B−/−) (Schoenfelder et al., 2015), most RYBP-repressed genes fell within the set of genes that are also regulated by RING1A/B (Figure 9B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison with published RING1A/B deletion data shown in Figure 9B

claim: The extent of gene reactivation at Polycomb target genes following RYBP removal is generally of lower magnitude than gene reactivation following deletion of RING1A/RING1B.
source: The extent of gene reactivation at Polycomb target genes following RYBP removalwas generally of lower magnitude than gene reactivation following deletion of RING1A/RING1B (Figure 9C), in agreement with our observations that RYBP stimulates, but is not absolutely required for, PRC1 activity and occupancy.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison shown in Figure 9C

claim: Increased transcription following RYBP loss is often coincident with TSS-associated decreases in PcG complex occupancy.
source: Indeed, when we examined individual RYBP-dependent genes, increased transcription was often coincident with TSS-associated decreases in PcG complex occupancy (Figure 9D), although this was more apparent for PRC1 than PRC2 (Figure 9E; Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by genomic snapshots and metaplots shown in Figures 9D and 9E

claim: There is a clear relationship between reduction of PRC1 occupancy at TSSs and increased gene expression following RYBP deletion.
source: When we extended this analysis genome-wide there was a very clear relationship, albeit not perfectly linear, between reduction of PRC1 occupancy at TSSs and increased gene expression (Figure 9F).
evidence: Demonstrated by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 9F

claim: The histone modifying activities of PRC1 and PRC2 underpin feedback mechanisms that are important for maintaining Polycomb chromatin domains, counteracting inappropriate gene activation signals, and shaping normal gene repression at a subset of polycomb target sites.
source: Furthermore it provides clear evidence that the histone modifying activities of PRC1 and PRC2 underpin feedback mechanisms that are important for maintaining Polycomb chromatin domains (Blackledge et al., 2015), counteracting inappropriate gene activation signals, and shaping normal gene repression, at least at a subset of polycomb target sites.
evidence: Concluded from combined analysis of histone modifications, PcG occupancy, and gene expression
